paras: The killing of Charles Flowers was the fatal shooting of a Black chain-gang convict by officers pursuing him after an escape near Savannah, Georgia, in December 1881. Flowers was wounded and recaptured at a camp about ten miles from the city and died at the Georgia Infirmary on the night of Wednesday, January 4, 1882. A coroner's jury found that he died of a gunshot wound from a gun held by one of his pursuers, John alias Samuel Golden, and called the killing manslaughter.

On December 14, 1881, the Police Court fined Flowers, whom the Savannah Morning News called "a notorious negro sneak thief," ten dollars or thirty days. On the evening of Thursday, December 15, he and two other Black men, convicted in several courts and sentenced to the chain gang, were turned over to convict guard T. B. Lee to be taken to the camp at Cuyler Swamp. About a mile out, according to the paper, the handcuffed prisoners knocked Lee down, took his key and pistol, freed themselves, and robbed him of sixty dollars and his watch.

Detectives employed by the County Commissioners set out with "an armed posse," according to the December 19 report; the January 7 report instead said the jailer, Waring Russell, sent "two officers." The pursuers found the escapees, with two Black men met on the road, camped near a railroad about ten miles out, waiting to board a train. In the December 19 version, the officers called on Flowers, William Henry alias Moon, and Robert Cummings to surrender and, when they ran, fired guns "loaded with small shot purposely" so as not to kill. Flowers, hit in the leg and body, was captured with eighteen dollars of the guard's money and his pistol; the other two got away, both wounded.

After Dr. J. G. Bulloch treated him at the jail, Flowers was moved on December 21 to the Georgia Infirmary, his condition "considered quite serious." He died there at about 11 o'clock on the night of January 4.

The coroner's inquest took testimony on January 5 and 6. The paper said the evidence matched its earlier account, but it also printed the sworn statement of John Flowers, the dead man's brother, treated as Charles's dying deposition. In it Charles denied any part in overpowering the guard and said a Mr. Jones shot him in the leg with a pistol, after which Golden fired one barrel of a gun into him and, when he begged "For God sake don't kill me!", the other while he lay in a ditch, until Jones asked whether he was "going to kill the man."

The eight-man jury, with Wm. W. Rogers as foreman, found that Flowers died of a gunshot wound from a gun in the hands of John alias Samuel Golden and declared, "we consider it manslaughter." No report of an arrest, indictment, or trial of Golden or Jones appears in the coverage.

All the coverage found came from the Savannah Morning News, which followed the case in its local columns for three weeks. It called Flowers "notorious" in nearly every item ("the notorious negro convict," "the notorious negro thief") and the escapees "rascals." Its first report of the shooting gave the officers' version without attribution and closed by praising the commissioners' "prompt act" and calling Flowers's recapture "a matter of gratulation."

Its assurance that Flowers was wounded "not seriously or dangerously" gave way to one-line notices of his transfer and death in the "Matters and Things Laconically Noted" column. The inquest report, headed "The Killed Convict," printed the brother's account and the manslaughter verdict in full without editorial comment.

The January 7 report dated the wounding to "the 21st of December," but the shooting was reported on December 19, placing it between December 15 and 18; December 21 was the day of his move to the infirmary. The December 19 report put the camp near the Central Railroad, while the inquest report placed it near the ten-mile post on the Charleston and Savannah Railway.
The officers' version described small shot fired at running men, while the brother's relayed statement described a pistol shot and two gun blasts after Flowers was down and pleading.

accounts.label: Officers' account (as printed by the paper)
accounts.gist: The officers called on the three escapees to surrender; when they ran, the officers fired guns loaded with small shot on purpose, not wishing to kill, and Flowers was wounded 'not seriously or dangerously' and captured.

accounts.label: Dying statement relayed by John Flowers
accounts.gist: Charles said he took no part in overpowering the guard; Jones shot him in the leg with a pistol, then Golden shot him with one barrel and, after he begged not to be killed, with the other while he lay in a ditch; Jones asked Golden if he was going to kill the man.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Flowers died of a gunshot wound from a gun in the hands of John alias Samuel Golden; the jury considered it manslaughter.

framing.detail: The first report relays the officers' version as fact, stresses 'small shot' fired 'purposely' to avoid killing, and calls the recapture of the 'most notorious' Flowers 'a matter of gratulation'.
The inquest report, headed 'The Killed Convict', prints the brother's statement and the manslaughter verdict in full without comment, while still calling Flowers 'the notorious negro thief'.
